update.draft:
MCP's Rise From Anthropic to Enterprise

In 2024, Anthropic announced the Model Context Protocol (MCP) with an ambitious goal: connecting AI applications like Claude and ChatGPT to external systems. This open-source standard became a critical tool for developers needing seamless integration between large language models (LLMs) and data sources without rewriting entire infrastructure.

From Launch To Standardization

The MCP protocol was designed as a standardized, two-way connection that enabled AI applications to interact with various tools and workflows. By creating universal rules for interaction between servers and clients, it eliminated the need for custom connectors in many scenarios. This standardization allowed developers to build once and deploy across multiple systems without rework.

Within its first year and a half, MCP underwent four significant spec revisions that refined how AI applications could communicate with external services through standardized protocols. These updates ensured compatibility between different platforms while maintaining the core functionality of connecting models to data sources efficiently.

A Stateless Revolution

The fifth revision marked a pivotal change: MCP went fully stateless, which simplified server architecture and improved scalability for enterprise use cases. This shift allowed developers to create more robust systems without worrying about session management or persistent connections between clients and servers.

This transformation was part of a broader trend where the protocol moved from being Anthropic-led toward cross-vendor agent infrastructure in less than two years. As MCP evolved, it became an open standard that could be adopted by multiple organizations working on AI integration projects without vendor lock-in or proprietary constraints.

Enterprise Adoption And Challenges

MCP's impact was evident as 28% of Fortune 500 companies deployed the protocol within a year. This rapid adoption demonstrated its value in reducing development time and costs by up to 400 custom connectors through solving what is known as the N×M Problem.

Despite these successes, MCP faced challenges including security concerns that raised red flags among enterprise users. Reports highlighted vulnerabilities such as GitHub's MCP server incidents which underscored the need for robust authentication mechanisms across all endpoints using this protocol.

Security And Governance

The National Security Agency (NSA) recognized these risks and outlined specific design considerations aimed at strengthening security within MCP infrastructure. These guidelines provided a framework that helped developers implement more secure practices when building servers or clients for AI integration tasks.

As the protocol matured, it attracted significant attention from both enterprise users looking to streamline their operations as well as researchers exploring ways to enhance its capabilities further through open collaboration under Linux Foundation governance since December 2025. This move ensured that MCP would continue evolving based on community input rather than being controlled by any single entity.
